claims.text: Premelting onset in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed primarily by surface chemical heterogeneity.
Full melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed primarily by surface chemical heterogeneity.
Local compositional disorder creates a distribution of surface bond strengths.
The distribution of surface bond strengths lowers the effective cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced surface cohesive energy triggers early, surface-initiated melting.
Surface-initiated melting subsequently propagates into the nanoparticle core.
As-synthesized high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have a random, well-mixed solid-solution structure.
As-synthesized high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles possess inherent surface chemical heterogeneity.
A post-synthesis annealing treatment can make the nanoparticle surface composition more homogeneous.
Surface regions having lower cohesive energy become liquid-like at lower temperatures than other regions.
Increasing surface compositional homogeneity makes local bond energies more uniform.
More uniform local surface bond energies raise the temperature required to initiate surface premelting.
More uniform local surface bond energies raise the overall melting temperature.
Surface-homogenized nanoparticles will exhibit higher premelting-onset temperatures than untreated nanoparticles of the same composition and size distribution.
Surface-homogenized nanoparticles will exhibit higher full-melting temperatures than untreated nanoparticles of the same composition and size distribution.
The proposed effect should occur for nanoparticles ranging from 5 to 50 nm in size.
The proposed effect should occur across high-entropy alloys containing four to five elements.
High-pressure or oxidative conditions may limit the applicability of the proposed mechanism.
Compositional segregation beyond that typical of a random solid solution may limit the applicability of the proposed mechanism.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in premelting and melting temperatures after verified surface homogenization would falsify the hypothesis.
